Introduction Manganese (Mn) is an essential trace element that is required to maintain a variety of metabolic and physiological functions in the body (Aschner and Aschner, 2005) since Mn is a cofactor for an array of metabolic and antioxidant enzymes such as glutamine synthetase and Mn superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) (Fridovich, 1974). Although Mn is vital for these biological functions, chronic exposure to excess Mn leads to a neurological condition referred to as manganism, which is characterized by pathological symptoms similar to those of Parkinson’s disease (PD) (Pal et al., 1999). Exposure to high levels of Mn may occur from various sources and means such as inhalation of particles from industrial emissions (Hassani et al., 2012), mining sites (Wang et al., 2018a), fertilizers (i.e., maneb, mancozeb) (de Tollenaer et al., 2006; Harrison Brody et al., 2013), gasoline additives [i.e., methylcyclopentadienyl Mn tricarbonyl (MMT)], as well as exposure to contaminated soil, water, and food sources (Arya and Roy, 2011; Okereafor et al., 2020). Given that these sources of Mn are ubiquitous in the environment, there is an increasing concern regarding the risk of Mn toxicity in the human population. Studies have shown that elevated levels of Mn in the brain of welders and smelters is correlated with higher risk of developing PD-like behavior and motor deficits (Juncos et al., 1968; Sriram et al., 2012). Moreover, Mn overexposure increased the risk of the development of abnormal behavior, cognitive decline and learning deficits in infants and children (Palzes et al., 2019; Rodrigues et al., 2018). In support of these findings, experimental studies have demonstrated that Mn impaired memory and learning ability in a mouse model (Song et al., 2016), along with pathological symptoms of locomotor activities (Alsulimani et al., 2015). Studies have reported that, in addition to basal ganglia, Mn accumulates in several other brain regions such as the frontal cortex, hippocampus and cerebellum upon its exposure (Garcia et al., 2006; Newland et al., 1989), suggesting that Mn may modulate a wide array of brain functions. Mn may be a risk factor for multiple neurological disorders including PD (Harischandra et al., 2019), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) (Tong et al., 2009) and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) (Guilarte, 2010). The underlying molecular mechanisms of Mn-induced neurotoxicity appear to be complex and may involve multiple mechanisms via various neural cell types in the brain, which ultimately deciphers Mn-induced neurotoxicity mechanisms. Studies have shown that mitochondrial impairment, oxidative stress, inflammation and excitotoxicity are involved in Mn-induced neurotoxicity (Brouillet et al., 1993; Gavin et al., 1990; Pajarillo et al., 2020; Popichak et al., 2018). Mitochondrial dysfunction may be an initiating event for Mn toxicity as Mn preferentially accumulates in mitochondria (Lai et al., 1999; Morello et al., 2008), leading to overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS), activation of proinflammatory signaling, and apoptotic cell death (Sarkar et al., 2018). Thus, understanding how Mn dysregulates these processes may provide invaluable information to prevent and treat neurodegenerative disorders associated with Mn-induced neurotoxicity. This review focuses on Mn-induced neurotoxicity mechanisms (Fig. 1) such as impairment of mitochondrial dynamics and mitophagy, autophagy dysregulation, oxidative and nitrosative stress, proinflammatory signaling and excitotoxicity, all of which eventually leads to Mn-induced neurotoxicity and behavioral consequences. We also discuss several genes involved in these cellular processes. 2. Effects of Mn on mitochondrial function Optimal mitochondrial function is critical for cell survival, and thus, toxic conditions that induce its impairment can lead to cellular injury. The proper functions of the mitochondria are maintained by the mitochondrial quality control (MQC) machinery, which is an integrated network of pathways involving mitochondrial dynamics, biogenesis and mitophagy (Palikaras et al., 2015). It has been shown that Mn accumulates in the mitochondria and impairs MQC machinery in neurons and astrocytes (Lai et al., 1999; Morello et al., 2008). Mn is mainly transported into the mitochondria via the mitochondrial Ca2+ uniporter system (Gunter et al., 1978; Puskin et al., 1976), suggesting that dysfunction of this transporter may lead to Mn accumulation in the mitochondria. Here, we will focus on Mn-induced dysfunction of mitochondrial fusion-fission dynamics and mitophagy degradation pathway. 2.1. Effects of Mn on mitochondrial fusion and fission Mitochondria are highly dynamic organelles that can build large interconnected intracellular networks (Bereiter-Hahn, 1990). Their shapes change continually through the combined actions of fission, fusion and motility. At the cellular level, mitochondrial fusion-fission dynamics are involved in maintenance of mitochondrial morphology, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) stability, respiratory capacity, apoptosis, and response to cellular stress (Chan, 2012). Proteins such as mitochondrial Rho GTPase 1 (MIRO1), mitofusin 1 (MFN1) and 2 (MFN2), dynamin-1-like protein (DLP1/DRP1), and optic atrophy 1 dynamin-like GTPase (OPA1) regulate mitochondrial fusion-fission process (Chang and Blackstone, 2010; Chen et al., 2003; Ishihara et al., 2004; Song et al., 2007, 2009). Published in final edited form as: Neurol Clin. 2020 Sep 12;38(4):913–936. doi: 10.1016/j.ncl.2020.07.008 INTRODUCTION Manganese (Mn) plays a critical role in many physiologic processes, including protein and energy metabolism, cellular protection from damaging free radicals, bone mineralization, immune function, reproduction, digestion, and metabolic regulation.1 Although vital in trace amounts, Mn overexposure has been associated with neurodegeneration and neurotoxicity.2 Chronic exposure to increased levels of Mn in occupational settings has resulted in a condition called manganism. Manganism is characterized by extrapyramidal symptoms, including bradykinesia, dystonia, gait instabilities, and speech impairments.3 In 1837, Dr John Couper first reported neurologic features associated with Mn exposure when several employees of a Mn processing facility presented with extrapyramidal symptoms. During the twentieth century, research remained focused on occupational exposure to Mn with workplace studies in industries such as welding, mining, and the manufacturing of Mn-containing products. In recent decades, research has become more focused on investigating the impact of chronic low-level exposure to Mn within the general population to understand the subsequent cognitive and neuromotor effects. In 1999, Mergler and colleagues2 were among the first to investigate the impact of low-level environmental exposure to Mn within a community setting. Subtle neurologic impairments were observed in relation to blood Mn levels. Current research builds on this concept by substantiating that lower-level environmental exposures are associated with subclinical neurologic effects.4 Abundant exposure to Mn occurs through diet,5 with factors such as age, gender, and nutritional status affecting absorption rates, which range from 1% to 5%.6 Although Mn is naturally present throughout the environment, anthropogenic sources such as industrial air pollution, agricultural fungicides, and gasoline additives contribute to the burden of excess environmental Mn. The inhalation of Mn is concerning because of greater absorption rates, especially within the brain.5 Homeostatic regulation is efficient at stabilizing levels of ingested Mn; however, airborne Mn may bypass these mechanisms and directly enter the brain by crossing the blood-brain barrier through membrane transporter proteins, transferrin and transferrin receptors,7 or via the olfactory nerve.8 Depending on the route of exposure, Mn absorption occurs via the gastrointestinal tract or lung with subsequent distribution throughout the body.9 The highest levels of Mn are reported in various organs, including the liver, bone, kidneys, pancreas, adrenal gland, and the pituitary gland within the brain.10 Typical levels of Mn in blood range from 4 to 15 μg/L.5 Circulating Mn is typically bound to hemoglobin; thus, the main compartment for Mn is the erythrocytes.11 The liver plays the primary role in the biological regulation of Mn by conjugating excess Mn to bile for excretion through the intestine.9 As indicated by the neurologic impairments associated with Mn exposure, the brain is very vulnerable to Mn toxicity. Mn accumulates in the brain with an affinity toward the basal ganglia structures.12 With a half-life estimated to be around 150 days, Mn has a slow clearance rate from the brain.13,14 In addition, it is thought that the high energy requirement and longevity of neurons contributes to enhanced neurologic susceptibility to Mn.9 This article examines the recent literature investigating the neurologic impact of Mn exposure on adult populations. This article synthesizes study findings to create a better understanding of the current state of research and to provide suggestions for future research directions. In 2016, a systematic review assessing Mn exposure and cognition across the lifespan was published.4 Thus, to incorporate the findings from current research into the discussion regarding adult Mn exposure and neurocognition, the authors searched for studies that were published between January 2016 and November 2019 investigating Mn exposure and neurocognition. We identified studies that met our criteria though PubMed and Medline using the following search terms: (manganese) AND (neurocognition OR cognition OR neuro) AND (adults) AND (occupation OR occupational OR environment OR environ*) (“2016/01/01”[Date – Publication]: “2019/11/01”[Date – Publication]). Previously, a review was published to assess the literature regarding Mn exposure and neuromotor outcomes.15 Therefore, we searched for studies that evaluated Mn exposure among adults and were published between November 2007 and November 2019. Studies that met our criteria were obtained using both PubMed and Medline and the following search terms: (manganese) AND (neurofunctional OR neuromotor OR motor OR neurobehavioral) AND (adults) AND (welders OR occupational OR occupational OR environ*) (“2007/07/ 01”[Date – Publication]: “2019/11/01”[Date – Publication]). Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2017 Dec 1. Published in final edited form as: Curr Environ Health Rep. 2016 Dec;3(4):392–404. doi: 10.1007/s40572-016-0108-x Abstract Manganese (Mn) is both an essential micronutrient and potential neurotoxicant. This dual role underlies a growing body of literature demonstrating that Mn exhibits a biphasic dose-response relationship with neurocognitive outcomes. We reviewed recent epidemiologic studies from 2007–2016 that investigated the relationship between Mn exposure and cognitive outcomes across the lifespan: early life, school-aged children, and adulthood. In total, 27 research articles were included in this review: 12 pediatric and 15 adult studies (10 occupational and five environmental exposures). The majority of these studies provided evidence of the negative effects of Mn exposure on cognition. The pediatric literature provides evidence that both high and low levels of Mn are negatively associated with intellectual development. Future Mn research should include examination of non-linear relationships and multiple neurotoxicants across the lifespan, and particularly during critical developmental windows. Keywords: pediatric, manganese, dose-response, literature review, occupational, cognition Introduction Manganese (Mn), an essential micronutrient, is required for the normal development of many organ systems and is crucial to brain growth and development [1, 2]. It is ubiquitous in the environment, naturally occurring in air, water, soil, and food [3]. Excess environmental exposure may arise from contaminated drinking water [4–6], air pollution [7–10], gasoline enhanced with methylcyclopentadienyl manganese tricarbonyl (MMT) [11], agricultural fungicides [12, 13], infant formulas [14], parenteral nutrition [15, 16], and illicit intravenous drug use [17]. Abundant in the diet, nutritional intake is the most common source for those who are not occupationally exposed [18]. Tight homeostatic mechanisms maintain adequate levels within the body through regulated gastrointestinal absorption and excretion [2]. To our knowledge, naturally occurring Mn deficiency has never been reported in humans; however, through experimentation in animal models and humans, inadequate Mn consumption has been associated with reproductive defects, weight loss, impaired growth, dermatological conditions, and altered mood [19, 20]. While Mn deficiency is a potential concern, overexposure may result in accumulation in the basal ganglia within the brain and thus, has been associated with adverse neurotoxic effects [21]. Many of the initial epidemiologic studies of Mn and health outcomes examined occupational inhalation exposures within industries such as ferromanganese welding, mining, and refining. In 1837, Couper was the first to document a Parkinson’s Disease-like syndrome in Mn poisoned Scottish Mn ore crushers [22] followed by Rodier in 1955 who further described Mn poisoning in Moroccan miners [23]. Elevated acute exposures to Mn have resulted in manganism, a condition characterized by Parkinsonian symptoms such as tremor, dystonia, and weakness [24]. Numerous biomarkers have been used to characterize internal dose measures of Mn. Given the essentiality of Mn for normal physiological function, it is understandable that each of these internal dose measures describe a unique aspect of Mn homeostasis. While blood Mn is the most commonly used biological indicator of Mn exposure, it may be more indicative of recent exposures rather than total body burden due to its short half-life and rapid hepatic clearance [28, 29]. Blood Mn may be best suited to characterize variability between subjects as opposed to within subjects [30]; therefore, blood Mn may be the most appropriate measure when comparing between exposed and unexposed populations. Hair Mn has been the most widely used biomarker of exposure with cognitive associations found for children [7–9, 31–33], and it may adequately characterize chronic low-level exposures [34]. Fingernails and toenails are non-invasive biological indicators of internal dose that have the potential to quantify longer-term exposure, ranging from seven to twelve months [39, 42, 43]. Abstract Occupational manganese exposure is associated with serious health concerns, ultimately leading to an illness called manganism. Competing meta-analytic results were published over a decade ago, ranging from undetectable to serious effects on cognitive performance among working adults. Novel studies and findings about the relationship between occupational manganese and cognitive functions have been proposed since. First of all, a systematic literature search was carried out until October 2022 via multiple electronic databases investigating the relationship between occupational manganese exposure and cognitive functions. Differences between the exposure and control groups in cognitive testing were synthesized by effect size Hedge's g. A random effects model was deployed with a restricted likelihood estimator using Hedges' invariance weighting. Publication bias, p-hacking and exposure-effect relationships were investigated. We included 18 studies with 75 effect sizes comparing n = 888 controls and 1092 exposed participants. After exclusion of outliers, we found significantly lower performances in processing speed, attention, working memory, reaction time, cognitive control and visual attention in workers exposed to manganese. Regression analysis revealed an indication of exposure-effect relationships between manganese exposure and cognitive functioning in exposed workers. We provide results of impaired cognitive functions for working adults exposed to manganese in processing speed, attention, working memory, reaction time and visual attention. Indications of quadratic exposure-effect relationships are discussed. We provide several recommendations for further studies to investigate possible exposure effects in the context of occupational health and safety. Despite its important physiological role, overexposure to this metal has been linked to serious health concerns (O'Neal & Zheng, 2015). Oral intake (e.g., drinking water) or inhalation (e.g., dust, fumes) are the main routes of absorption. When manganese enters the biological system, it accumulates in the liver and bones, but mostly in the human brain, unfolding neurotoxic effects (O'Neal & Zheng, 2015). Studies suggest that manganese, among other metals such as lead, may accumulate in the brain via olfactory pathways, impairing not only olfactory functioning but also cognitive functioning (Tzivian et al., 2016; Guarneros et al., 2020). Intoxication through manganese was first documented in association with poisoned ore workers, describing the illness as manganism, resembling symptoms of Parkinson's disease (Couper, 1837; Zoni et al., 2007). Additionally, recent studies have associated decreased motor functioning with higher exposure to manganese (Lotz et al., 2021). Since the metal is still used in various industrial processes (e.g., smelting, welding, mining, alloy production), it poses a possible risk factor to humans to this day. Some epidemiological studies have focused on environmental exposure; however, most results regarding the toxic effect of manganese are based on occupational exposure (O'Neal & Zheng, 2015). Due to their chronic exposure to manganese, workers in industrial fields (e.g., smelters, welders) form a special group at risk of adverse health effects. Occupational exposure to manganese has been related to damage to the central and vegetative nervous system resulting in impairments of organs (Harischandra et al., 2019). The association between manganese exposure and cognitive functioning has been the focus of research on workplace health and safety. Although multiple biomarkers for manganese exposure have been proposed (e.g., bone, hair and nails), three main assessments are consistently used by occupational studies (Martin et al., 2020). First, blood manganese levels in microgram per litre (BloodMn μg/L) are analyzed when short-term or acute effects of exposure are of interest. Observational evidence on manganese exposure and cognitive outcomes indicates that higher exposure is generally associated with worse cognition, though the strength and consistency of the association vary across studies and populations. The evidence base spans occupational and environmental exposures, with a strong emphasis on adults and children.

Across adult populations, systematic reviews and meta-analyses consistently find that occupational manganese exposure is linked to cognitive deficits. A meta-analysis of 18 studies found significantly lower cognitive performance in manganese-exposed workers in processing speed, attention, working memory, reaction time, cognitive control, and visual attention [N4-F4]. Another systematic review on manganese exposure and adult neurologic outcomes also states that occupational exposure has been associated with neurodegeneration and neurotoxicity, and that lower-level environmental exposures are associated with subclinical neurologic effects [N2-F2]. In the same adult review, the authors note that blood manganese is a common biomarker, though it may better reflect recent exposure than total body burden [N2-F2].

For children, the evidence is similarly consistent but more mixed in interpretation. A review of manganese exposure and cognition across the lifespan reports that both high and low levels of Mn are negatively associated with intellectual development in children [N4-R1]. Another review notes that higher manganese exposure in children is associated with poorer cognitive performance, especially in the verbal domain [N5-R2]. However, one study in school-age children in rural eastern Ohio found elevated manganese exposure associated with poorer cognitive performance, supporting a negative exposure-outcome relationship [N5-R1]. A separate review also emphasizes that Mn exposure in children is typically characterized by non-linear associations and that future research should examine non-linear relationships across the lifespan [N4-F4].

Blood manganese levels do track cognitive decline across studies, but the relationship is not uniform. In a study of elderly subjects, higher whole blood manganese was associated with cognitive decline in the highest quartile (>11.8 μg/L) [N4-R5]. In a review of Mn exposure and cognition across the lifespan, blood Mn is described as the most commonly used biological indicator, but it may be better suited for comparing between exposed and unexposed populations than for capturing within-subject variability [N3-F3]. This suggests that blood manganese can indicate exposure-related cognitive risk, but its value depends on whether the study is comparing groups rather than tracking longitudinal change over time.

Exposure timing and duration shape the association in important ways. Occupational exposures are often chronic and long-term, and the evidence base includes both short-term and long-term exposure assessments [N4-F4]. The meta-analysis used personal inhalable manganese exposure during working hours and cumulative exposure indices, showing that long-term exposure effects were consistently associated with worse cognitive performance [N4-F4]. The same review also notes that blood manganese may be more informative for short-term effects, whereas cumulative exposure indices better reflect long-term exposure effects [N4-F4]. In children, exposure timing matters because the review argues that non-linear relationships may emerge across different developmental windows, and that Mn exposure during early life can affect later cognitive outcomes [N4-F4]. This aligns with findings in school-age children and adolescents, where early-life exposure has been linked to verbal learning and memory [N5-R3].

Overall, the observational evidence supports a general association between higher manganese exposure and worse cognition, with blood manganese levels often tracking cognitive decline. However, the association is not always linear, and exposure classification varies by study design and population. Blood manganese is useful as a biomarker, but it has limitations in inferring long-term exposure because it reflects recent exposure and may be influenced by homeostatic clearance [N3-F3][N4-F4].

The biological pathway evidence indicates that manganese affects cognition through a broad set of neurotoxic mechanisms, with the basal ganglia, frontal cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum being the brain regions most directly implicated. The mechanisms are primarily oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and autophagy dysregulation.

First, the evidence repeatedly points to the basal ganglia as a central target. A review states that Mn accumulates in the brain with an affinity toward basal ganglia structures, and that chronic exposure can result in neurodegeneration and neurotoxicity [N2-F2]. Another review explicitly notes that Mn accumulates in the basal ganglia and is associated with Parkinsonian symptoms, including bradykinesia, dystonia, and gait instabilities [N2-F2]. The same review also reports that Mn accumulates in other brain regions such as the frontal cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum, suggesting a broader impact on brain function [N2-F2]. This is supported by mechanistic studies showing that Mn may impair synaptic function and induce mitochondrial dysfunction [N1-R4].

Oxidative stress is a central mechanism. The review on manganese neurotoxicity mechanisms explicitly states that Mn-induced neurotoxicity involves oxidative stress and that oxidative stress contributes to cellular dysfunction and disease [N1-R5]. It also notes that Mn can lead to overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS), activation of proinflammatory signaling, and apoptotic cell death [N1-F1]. Another review states that Mn-induced oxidative stress and nitrosative stress are implicated in Mn neurotoxicity [N1-R5]. This indicates that oxidative stress is not just a downstream consequence but a core driver of Mn toxicity.

Inflammation is also implicated. The same review states that Mn toxicity activates proinflammatory signaling and contributes to apoptotic cell death [N1-F1]. This means that Mn exposure can trigger an inflammatory response in the brain, which may amplify tissue damage and neurodegeneration.

Mitochondrial dysfunction is another major pathway. The review on manganese neurotoxicity mechanisms explains that mitochondrial impairment is an initiating event for Mn toxicity because Mn preferentially accumulates in mitochondria [N1-F1]. It further notes that Mn impairs mitochondrial quality control (MQC) machinery in neurons and astrocytes, disrupts mitochondrial fusion-fission dynamics, and affects mitophagy degradation pathways [N1-F1]. The same evidence base also states that Mn is transported into the mitochondria via the mitochondrial Ca2+ uniporter system and that dysfunction of this transporter may lead to Mn accumulation in mitochondria [N1-F1]. This creates a strong loop: Mn accumulation in mitochondria leads to mitochondrial dysfunction, which in turn exacerbates oxidative stress and inflammation.

Autophagy dysregulation is another important mechanism. The review states that autophagy dysregulation is involved in Mn-induced neurotoxicity [N1-R1]. This suggests that the cell’s ability to clear damaged mitochondria and other debris is compromised under Mn exposure, worsening neurotoxicity.

Evidence for dose-dependent or threshold-dependent neurotoxicity is mixed but suggestive of a non-linear pattern. The review on manganese exposure and cognition across the lifespan argues for a biphasic dose-response relationship, in which both high and low levels of Mn are negatively associated with intellectual development [N4-R1]. The meta-analysis on occupational manganese exposure also notes that quadratic exposure-effect models performed better than linear models, indicating that the relationship may be curvilinear [N4-F4]. This supports the idea that Mn neurotoxicity is not simply monotonic but may depend on exposure level, with both low and high exposures potentially harming cognition. The review also emphasizes that future research should examine non-linear relationships and multiple neurotoxicants across the lifespan [N4-F4].

Taken together, the biological pathway evidence indicates that manganese affects cognition through a complex interplay of oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and autophagy dysregulation, primarily targeting the basal ganglia and other limbic and executive brain regions. The evidence also supports the possibility of a biphasic or nonlinear dose-response relationship, meaning that both low and high exposures can be harmful [N1-R1][N1-R5][N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-F4].

The severity and interpretation evidence suggest that the relationship between manganese and cognitive impairment is not simply linear, and that cognitive domains, severity measurement, and biomarker utility differ across studies. The evidence also indicates that non-linear or threshold-dependent effects are plausible, especially in children and adolescents.

Evidence for linear versus nonlinear relationships is strongest in the pediatric literature. A review on manganese exposure and cognition across the lifespan explicitly states that both high and low levels of Mn are negatively associated with intellectual development, supporting a non-linear or biphasic pattern [N4-R1]. The same review argues that future research should examine non-linear relationships and multiple neurotoxicants across the lifespan [N4-F4]. Another meta-analysis of occupational manganese exposure reports that quadratic exposure-effect models performed better than linear models, further suggesting a non-linear relationship [N4-F4]. This pattern implies that cognitive impairment may increase with both low and high Mn exposure, rather than only at very high levels.

The cognitive domains most affected appear to vary by age group and exposure context. In adults, the meta-analysis found impaired cognitive performance in processing speed, attention, working memory, reaction time, cognitive control, and visual attention [N4-F4]. In children, the evidence points to verbal cognitive domains as especially vulnerable. A study of school-age children found that high manganese exposure was associated with poorer cognitive performance, especially in the verbal domain [N5-R2]. Another study in rural eastern Ohio children found elevated manganese exposure associated with poorer cognitive performance, supporting verbal deficits in this age group [N5-R1]. A more recent study on early-life manganese exposure also found associations with adolescent verbal learning and memory, indicating that verbal domains may be a consistent vulnerability across developmental stages [N5-R3]. This suggests that verbal cognition is a particularly sensitive endpoint, while processing speed and attention are more frequently reported in adult occupational studies [N4-F4].

Severity is measured in several ways across the studies. In adults, cognitive performance is usually assessed through standardized neuropsychological tests and compared across exposed versus unexposed groups [N4-F4]. In children, cognitive outcomes are often measured using tests of intellectual development, verbal performance, processing speed, and attention [N5-R1][N5-R2]. The review on manganese exposure and cognition across the lifespan also notes that cognitive outcomes are evaluated in early life, school-aged children, and adults, with the pediatric literature showing negative associations with intellectual development [N4-F4]. This indicates that severity is typically operationalized as poorer cognitive test scores rather than as a single global impairment measure.

Biomarkers add value in several ways. Blood manganese is the most commonly used biomarker in occupational and environmental studies, and it is useful for comparing exposed and unexposed populations [N3-F3]. However, the review notes that blood Mn may be more indicative of recent exposure than total body burden [N3-F3]. Hair manganese and other biomarkers are also discussed as possible alternatives, with hair Mn being used for children and long-term exposure assessment [N3-F3]. The review also notes that biomarkers help capture internal dose measurements and reduce reporting bias in epidemiologic studies [N3-F3]. Thus, biomarkers are valuable because they provide a more objective exposure measure than self-reported or environmental proxies, but their usefulness depends on the study question: blood Mn is better for recent exposure, while other biomarkers may be better for cumulative exposure or long-term assessment [N3-F3][N4-F4].

In summary, the evidence supports a non-linear or threshold-dependent relationship between manganese and cognitive impairment, with verbal domains especially vulnerable in children and adolescents, and processing speed, attention, and working memory frequently impaired in adults. Severity is typically measured through standardized cognitive tests, and biomarkers add value by capturing internal exposure and reducing bias, though they also have limitations in inferring long-term exposure [N4-R1][N4-F4][N5-R2][N5-R3][N3-F3].

Blood manganese measurement and exposure classification are central to interpreting manganese-cognition associations, but the evidence also highlights important limitations. Across the studies, normal and elevated blood manganese levels are not universally standardized, and exposure classification varies by population, study design, and exposure route.

Blood manganese levels are generally considered normal within a range that reflects homeostatic regulation. The review on manganese exposure and cognition across the lifespan states that typical blood Mn levels range from 4 to 15 μg/L [N3-F3]. In the same source, it notes that circulating Mn is typically bound to hemoglobin, with the main compartment being erythrocytes [N3-F3]. This suggests that blood manganese is a dynamic measure influenced by recent exposure and clearance, rather than a stable long-term indicator. The review also states that blood Mn may be best suited for characterizing variability between subjects rather than within subjects, and that it may be most appropriate when comparing exposed and unexposed populations [N3-F3].

Elevated blood manganese is more context-dependent. The review identifies elevated Mn as being associated with cognitive decline in elderly subjects in the highest quartile (>11.8 μg/L) [N4-R5]. However, the normal range from the same source is 4–15 μg/L, so “elevated” is not a fixed threshold across all populations or exposure contexts. The meta-analysis also notes that blood manganese may be more indicative of recent exposure, while cumulative exposure indices better reflect long-term exposure [N4-F4]. This means that a single blood Mn measurement cannot reliably distinguish acute, subacute, or chronic exposure.

Exposure is classified across studies and populations in several ways. Occupational studies often use blood manganese as a biomarker, along with airborne inhalable manganese and cumulative exposure indices [N4-F4]. The meta-analysis distinguishes between blood Mn, airborne inhalable Mn, and cumulative exposure indices, and notes that these biomarkers capture different aspects of exposure: blood Mn for short-term or recent effects, airborne inhalable Mn for workplace exposure, and cumulative exposure indices for long-term effects [N4-F4]. In non-occupational or environmental studies, the review notes that exposure biomarkers such as blood Mn may not fully capture internal dose, and that other biomarkers such as hair Mn, nails, and MnRBCs have been used to characterize chronic low-level exposures [N3-F3]. The same review also mentions that urine Mn is not recommended because only slight levels are eliminated in urine due to primary biliary excretion [N3-F3].

Limitations of using blood manganese to infer long-term exposure are substantial. The review states that blood Mn is the most commonly used biological indicator, but it may be more indicative of recent exposures rather than total body burden due to its short half-life and rapid hepatic clearance [N3-F3]. It also says that blood Mn may be best suited for comparing between exposed and unexposed populations rather than for within-subject variability [N3-F3]. Another source notes that blood manganese as a biomarker remains controversial because it reflects recent exposure and is difficult to interpret for chronic exposure [N6-R2]. In occupational studies, the review further explains that blood Mn may be used for short-term or acute effects, while cumulative exposure indices better reflect long-term exposure effects [N4-F4].

Overall, blood manganese levels are considered normal within a range of approximately 4–15 μg/L, but “elevated” is context-dependent and not universally standardized [N3-F3][N4-R5]. Exposure is classified across studies using blood Mn, airborne inhalable Mn, cumulative exposure indices, hair Mn, nails, MnRBCs, and other biomarkers, depending on the study design and exposure context [N3-F3][N4-F4]. However, blood manganese has limitations for long-term exposure inference because it reflects recent exposure and may not capture cumulative or chronic exposure well [N3-F3][N4-F4].

## How are blood manganese levels related to the severity of cognitive impairment?

The relationship between blood manganese levels and the severity of cognitive impairment is best understood as a complex, multi-level association: manganese exposure can impair cognition through biological pathways, observational studies show worse outcomes at higher exposure, severity varies by cognitive domain and exposure pattern, and blood manganese itself is a useful but imperfect biomarker.

---

## 1) Biological pathways: manganese affects cognition through multiple neurotoxic mechanisms

The evidence indicates that manganese affects cognition primarily through oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and autophagy dysregulation. Manganese accumulates in brain regions that are central to motor control, executive function, and memory, including the **basal ganglia, frontal cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum** [N2-F2][N1-F1]. This accumulation is especially relevant because the brain is vulnerable to manganese toxicity: Mn preferentially enters mitochondria, where it disrupts mitochondrial quality control, fusion-fission dynamics, and mitophagy [N1-F1]. That mitochondrial impairment then leads to **oxidative stress** and **reactive oxygen species/nitrosative stress**, which activate proinflammatory signaling and can drive apoptotic cell death [N1-F1][N1-R5]. In other words, manganese toxicity is not a single-step process; it unfolds through a cascade of cellular dysregulation.

The evidence also supports a **non-linear or biphasic dose-response pattern**. The manganese exposure and cognition review explicitly states that both high and low levels of Mn are negatively associated with intellectual development [N4-R1], while the occupational manganese meta-analysis found that quadratic exposure-effect models performed better than linear models [N4-F4]. This suggests that both low and high exposures can be harmful, and the relationship is not simply monotonic. Taken together, the biological pathway evidence indicates that manganese severity is mediated by brain-region-specific toxicity, with oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and autophagy dysregulation as the major mechanisms [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R5][N4-R1][N4-F4].

---

## 2) Observational evidence: higher manganese exposure is generally associated with worse cognition

Across occupational and environmental studies, the observational evidence consistently points to an association between higher manganese exposure and worse cognitive outcomes. A meta-analysis of 18 occupational studies found significantly lower cognitive performance in manganese-exposed workers in **processing speed, attention, working memory, reaction time, cognitive control, and visual attention** [N4-F4]. For children, the evidence is equally consistent. The manganese exposure and cognition review reports that both high and low levels of Mn are negatively associated with intellectual development in children [N4-R1]. A more recent study on early-life manganese exposure also found associations with **adolescent verbal learning and memory** [N5-R3]. These findings support the idea that manganese can impair cognition across the lifespan and that the cognitive endpoints vary by age.

---

## 3) Blood manganese levels track cognitive decline across studies, but with important caveats

Blood manganese levels do appear to track cognitive decline in several studies. In elderly subjects, higher whole blood manganese was associated with cognitive decline in the highest quartile (>11.8 μg/L) [N4-R5]. In occupational studies, blood manganese is the most commonly used biomarker and is useful for comparing exposed versus unexposed populations [N3-F3]. However, it is not a perfect measure of long-term exposure. The same review notes that blood manganese may reflect **recent exposure** rather than total body burden, and that it is more indicative of short-term variability than within-subject change over time [N3-F3]. That is why occupational studies also use airborne inhalable manganese and cumulative exposure indices to better capture long-term exposure effects [N4-F4].

The evidence therefore suggests a useful but limited role for blood manganese: it is helpful for identifying exposure-related cognitive risk and for comparing groups, but it should not be used alone to infer cumulative or chronic exposure [N3-F3][N4-F4]. Blood manganese is especially useful in occupational settings where recent exposure is the main concern, while other biomarkers may be better suited for chronic or developmental exposure assessment [N3-F3].

---

## 4) Severity gradients: the relationship is nonlinear, and cognitive domains differ

The severity evidence suggests that the relationship between manganese and cognitive impairment is not simply linear. The pediatric literature indicates that both high and low levels of Mn are associated with negative intellectual outcomes, supporting a **non-linear or threshold-dependent pattern** [N4-R1][N4-F4]. This means that manganese can impair cognition at both low and high exposure levels, and that there may be a "safe" range in between.

Cognitive domains affected also differ by age and exposure context. In adults, the meta-analysis found impaired performance in **processing speed, attention, working memory, reaction time, cognitive control, and visual attention** [N4-F4]. This suggests that verbal domains are especially sensitive in younger populations, while processing speed and attention are more frequently reported in adult occupational studies.

Severity is typically measured through standardized cognitive tests and compared across exposed and unexposed groups [N4-F4]. In children, outcomes are often measured using tests of intellectual development, verbal performance, and attention [N5-R1][N5-R2]. Biomarkers add value by capturing internal dose and reducing reporting bias, but they also have limitations: blood manganese is best suited for recent exposure and group comparisons, while other biomarkers may be better for long-term or cumulative exposure [N3-F3][N4-F4].

---

## 5) Measurement and exposure classification: blood manganese is useful but imperfect

Blood manganese is usually considered normal within a range of **4 to 15 μg/L**, with elevated levels associated with cognitive decline in the highest quartile (>11.8 μg/L) [N3-F3][N4-R5]. A key limitation of blood manganese is that it reflects **recent exposure** rather than long-term burden. Because Mn is rapidly cleared by the liver and has a short half-life, blood levels may not capture chronic or cumulative exposure well [N3-F3][N4-F4]. This means that a single blood manganese measurement may underestimate long-term exposure and therefore underestimate true cognitive risk.

## 6) Integrated conclusion

Overall, the evidence supports a **graded relationship** between blood manganese levels and cognitive impairment severity: higher manganese exposure is generally associated with worse cognition, but the association is not uniform or linear [N4-R1][N4-F4]. The biological pathway evidence shows that Mn toxicity operates through multiple mechanisms, including oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and autophagy dysregulation, and that it affects brain regions such as the basal ganglia, frontal cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R5]. Observational studies find worse cognitive outcomes in adults and children exposed to manganese, with verbal domains especially vulnerable in younger populations [N4-F4][N5-R2][N5-R3]. ## How are blood manganese levels related to the severity of cognitive impairment?

The relationship between blood manganese levels and the severity of cognitive impairment is best understood as a complex, multi-level association: manganese exposure can impair cognition through biological pathways, observational studies show worse outcomes at higher exposure, severity varies by cognitive domain and exposure pattern, and blood manganese itself is a useful but imperfect biomarker.

---

## 1) Biological pathways: manganese affects cognition through multiple neurotoxic mechanisms

The evidence indicates that manganese affects cognition primarily through oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and autophagy dysregulation. Manganese accumulates in brain regions that are central to motor control, executive function, and memory, including the **basal ganglia, frontal cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum** [N2-F2][N1-F1]. This accumulation is especially relevant because the brain is vulnerable to manganese toxicity: Mn preferentially enters mitochondria, where it disrupts mitochondrial quality control, fusion-fission dynamics, and mitophagy [N1-F1]. That mitochondrial impairment then leads to **oxidative stress** and **reactive oxygen species/nitrosative stress**, which activate proinflammatory signaling and can drive apoptotic cell death [N1-F1][N1-R5]. In other words, manganese toxicity is not a single-step process; it unfolds through a cascade of cellular dysregulation.

The evidence also supports a **non-linear or biphasic dose-response pattern**. The manganese exposure and cognition review explicitly states that both high and low levels of Mn are negatively associated with intellectual development [N4-R1], while the occupational manganese meta-analysis found that quadratic exposure-effect models performed better than linear models [N4-F4]. This suggests that both low and high exposures can be harmful, and the relationship is not simply monotonic. Taken together, the biological pathway evidence indicates that manganese severity is mediated by brain-region-specific toxicity, with oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and autophagy dysregulation as the major mechanisms [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R5][N4-R1][N4-F4].

---

## 2) Observational evidence: higher manganese exposure is generally associated with worse cognition

Across occupational and environmental studies, the observational evidence consistently points to an association between higher manganese exposure and worse cognitive outcomes. A meta-analysis of 18 occupational studies found significantly lower cognitive performance in manganese-exposed workers in **processing speed, attention, working memory, reaction time, cognitive control, and visual attention** [N4-F4]. A systematic review of manganese exposure and adult neurologic outcomes similarly concluded that occupational exposure is associated with neurodegeneration and neurotoxicity, and that lower-level environmental exposures are associated with subclinical neurologic effects [N2-F2]. This means that manganese is not only a concern for acute or high-level poisoning but also for chronic low-level exposure.

For children, the evidence is equally consistent. The manganese exposure and cognition review reports that both high and low levels of Mn are negatively associated with intellectual development in children [N4-R1]. Another study found that higher manganese exposure in children is associated with poorer cognitive performance, especially in the **verbal domain** [N5-R2], while a rural school-age cohort study found elevated manganese exposure associated with poorer cognitive performance [N5-R1]. A more recent study on early-life manganese exposure also found associations with **adolescent verbal learning and memory** [N5-R3]. These findings support the idea that manganese can impair cognition across the lifespan and that the cognitive endpoints vary by age.

---

## 3) Blood manganese levels track cognitive decline across studies, but with important caveats

Blood manganese levels do appear to track cognitive decline in several studies. In elderly subjects, higher whole blood manganese was associated with cognitive decline in the highest quartile (>11.8 μg/L) [N4-R5]. In occupational studies, blood manganese is the most commonly used biomarker and is useful for comparing exposed versus unexposed populations [N3-F3]. However, it is not a perfect measure of long-term exposure. The same review notes that blood manganese may reflect **recent exposure** rather than total body burden, and that it is more indicative of short-term variability than within-subject change over time [N3-F3]. That is why occupational studies also use airborne inhalable manganese and cumulative exposure indices to better capture long-term exposure effects [N4-F4].

The evidence therefore suggests a useful but limited role for blood manganese: it is helpful for identifying exposure-related cognitive risk and for comparing groups, but it should not be used alone to infer cumulative or chronic exposure [N3-F3][N4-F4]. Blood manganese is especially useful in occupational settings where recent exposure is the main concern, while other biomarkers may be better suited for chronic or developmental exposure assessment [N3-F3].

---

## 4) Severity gradients: the relationship is nonlinear, and cognitive domains differ

The severity evidence suggests that the relationship between manganese and cognitive impairment is not simply linear. The pediatric literature indicates that both high and low levels of Mn are associated with negative intellectual outcomes, supporting a **non-linear or threshold-dependent pattern** [N4-R1][N4-F4]. This means that manganese can impair cognition at both low and high exposure levels, and that there may be a "safe" range in between.

Cognitive domains affected also differ by age and exposure context. In adults, the meta-analysis found impaired performance in **processing speed, attention, working memory, reaction time, cognitive control, and visual attention** [N4-F4]. In children, the most consistently affected domains are **verbal cognition**, with evidence from school-age children showing poorer cognitive performance in the verbal domain [N5-R2], and from adolescents showing associations with **verbal learning and memory** [N5-R3]. This suggests that verbal domains are especially sensitive in younger populations, while processing speed and attention are more frequently reported in adult occupational studies.

Severity is typically measured through standardized cognitive tests and compared across exposed and unexposed groups [N4-F4]. In children, outcomes are often measured using tests of intellectual development, verbal performance, and attention [N5-R1][N5-R2]. Biomarkers add value by capturing internal dose and reducing reporting bias, but they also have limitations: blood manganese is best suited for recent exposure and group comparisons, while other biomarkers may be better for long-term or cumulative exposure [N3-F3][N4-F4].

---

## 5) Measurement and exposure classification: blood manganese is useful but imperfect

Blood manganese is usually considered normal within a range of **4 to 15 μg/L**, with elevated levels associated with cognitive decline in the highest quartile (>11.8 μg/L) [N3-F3][N4-R5]. However, normal ranges are not universally standardized, and “elevated” is context-dependent [N3-F3]. Exposure classification also varies across studies: occupational studies often use **blood manganese, airborne inhalable manganese, and cumulative exposure indices** [N4-F4]. Environmental and non-occupational studies may rely on other biomarkers such as hair manganese, nails, MnRBCs, and urine Mn, though urine Mn is not recommended because only small amounts are excreted [N3-F3].

A key limitation of blood manganese is that it reflects **recent exposure** rather than long-term burden. Because Mn is rapidly cleared by the liver and has a short half-life, blood levels may not capture chronic or cumulative exposure well [N3-F3][N4-F4]. This means that a single blood manganese measurement may underestimate long-term exposure and therefore underestimate true cognitive risk.

---

## 6) Integrated conclusion

Overall, the evidence supports a **graded relationship** between blood manganese levels and cognitive impairment severity: higher manganese exposure is generally associated with worse cognition, but the association is not uniform or linear [N4-R1][N4-F4]. The biological pathway evidence shows that Mn toxicity operates through multiple mechanisms, including oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and autophagy dysregulation, and that it affects brain regions such as the basal ganglia, frontal cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R5]. Observational studies find worse cognitive outcomes in adults and children exposed to manganese, with verbal domains especially vulnerable in younger populations [N4-F4][N5-R2][N5-R3]. Blood manganese levels do track cognitive decline, but they are best interpreted as a recent-exposure biomarker rather than a long-term exposure indicator [N3-F3][N4-F4].

The manganese exposure and cognition review explicitly states that both high and low levels of Mn are negatively associated with intellectual development [N4-R1], while the occupational manganese meta-analysis found that quadratic exposure-effect models performed better than linear models [N4-F4]. Across occupational and environmental studies, the observational evidence consistently points to an association between higher manganese exposure and worse cognitive outcomes. This means that manganese is not only a concern for acute or high-level poisoning but also for chronic low-level exposure.

The manganese exposure and cognition review reports that both high and low levels of Mn are negatively associated with intellectual development in children [N4-R1]. Blood manganese levels do appear to track cognitive decline in several studies. The evidence therefore suggests a useful but limited role for blood manganese: it is helpful for identifying exposure-related cognitive risk and for comparing groups, but it should not be used alone to infer cumulative or chronic exposure [N3-F3][N4-F4]. Blood manganese is especially useful in occupational settings where recent exposure is the main concern, while other biomarkers may be better suited for chronic or developmental exposure assessment [N3-F3].

---

## 4) Severity gradients: the relationship is nonlinear, and cognitive domains differ

The severity evidence suggests that the relationship between manganese and cognitive impairment is not simply linear. The pediatric literature indicates that both high and low levels of Mn are associated with negative intellectual outcomes, supporting a **non-linear or threshold-dependent pattern** [N4-R1][N4-F4]. This means that manganese can impair cognition at both low and high exposure levels, and that there may be a "safe" range in between.

Cognitive domains affected also differ by age and exposure context. In adults, the meta-analysis found impaired performance in **processing speed, attention, working memory, reaction time, cognitive control, and visual attention** [N4-F4]. In children, the most consistently affected domains are **verbal cognition**, with evidence from school-age children showing poorer cognitive performance in the verbal domain [N5-R2], and from adolescents showing associations with **verbal learning and memory** [N5-R3]. This suggests that verbal domains are especially sensitive in younger populations, while processing speed and attention are more frequently reported in adult occupational studies.

Severity is typically measured through standardized cognitive tests and compared across exposed and unexposed groups [N4-F4]. In children, outcomes are often measured using tests of intellectual development, verbal performance, and attention [N5-R1][N5-R2]. Biomarkers add value by capturing internal dose and reducing reporting bias, but they also have limitations: blood manganese is best suited for recent exposure and group comparisons, while other biomarkers may be better for long-term or cumulative exposure [N3-F3][N4-F4].

---

## 5) Measurement and exposure classification: blood manganese is useful but imperfect

Blood manganese is usually considered normal within a range of **4 to 15 μg/L**, with elevated levels associated with cognitive decline in the highest quartile (>11.8 μg/L) [N3-F3][N4-R5]. However, normal ranges are not universally standardized, and “elevated” is context-dependent [N3-F3]. Exposure classification also varies across studies: occupational studies often use **blood manganese, airborne inhalable manganese, and cumulative exposure indices** [N4-F4]. Environmental and non-occupational studies may rely on other biomarkers such as hair manganese, nails, MnRBCs, and urine Mn, though urine Mn is not recommended because only small amounts are excreted [N3-F3].

A key limitation of blood manganese is that it reflects **recent exposure** rather than long-term burden. Because Mn is rapidly cleared by the liver and has a short half-life, blood levels may not capture chronic or cumulative exposure well [N3-F3][N4-F4]. This means that a single blood manganese measurement may underestimate long-term exposure and therefore underestimate true cognitive risk.

---

## 6) Integrated conclusion

Overall, the evidence supports a **graded relationship** between blood manganese levels and cognitive impairment severity: higher manganese exposure is generally associated with worse cognition, but the association is not uniform or linear [N4-R1][N4-F4]. The biological pathway evidence shows that Mn toxicity operates through multiple mechanisms, including oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and autophagy dysregulation, and that it affects brain regions such as the basal ganglia, frontal cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R5]. Observational studies find worse cognitive outcomes in adults and children exposed to manganese, with verbal domains especially vulnerable in younger populations [N4-F4][N5-R2][N5-R3]. Blood manganese levels do track cognitive decline, but they are best interpreted as a recent-exposure biomarker rather than a long-term exposure indicator [N3-F3][N4-F4].
